title: Exact Change at the Ticket Booth
statement:
You sell tickets that cost 5 each. Customers arrive one at a time in the order given by bills, and each pays with a single note of 5, 10 or 20. You start with an empty till, and you can only hand out notes that earlier customers gave you.

Every customer must get exact change right away. Return true if you can serve everyone, and false as soon as some customer cannot be given change.

examples.why: After two 5s you hold 5, 5. The 10 takes one 5 back. The 20 gets the 10 and the last 5.
Pay the 20 with 10 + 5, not 5 + 5 + 5. Keeping 5s lets you serve the two 10s that come after.
The first 20 uses the 10 and a 5. The second 20 needs 15, but only one 5 is left.

hints: You only ever need to know how many 5s and how many 10s are in the till. 20s are never given back as change.
A 10 always needs one 5 back. A 20 needs 15 back, which can be 10 + 5 or 5 + 5 + 5.
When paying out 15, use the 10 if you have one. A 5 can make change for both 10s and 20s, a 10 only for 20s, so 5s are the notes to save.

explain.intuition:
Simulate the till. The only real decision is how to pay 15 to a customer with a 20: one 10 plus one 5, or three 5s. Always spend the 10 first. A 5 is the more useful note: it is the only change for a 10, and it also works for a 20. A 10 is useful only for a 20. Spending the less flexible note never leaves you worse off.

It is the same reasoning as picking which cache entry to evict: throw out the one that can serve fewer future requests.
steps: For a 10: if fives == 0 return false; else take one five and add one ten.
For a 20: if you have a ten and a five, take one of each; else if you have three fives, take three; else return false.
pitfalls: Paying 15 with three 5s when a 10 is available. In the second example that strands the later customers who pay with 10.
Counting the 20s as usable change. They never help, since no customer needs more than 15 back.
Checking only the total money in the till. 20 in the till as a single note cannot make 5 of change.

solutions.title: Count fives and tens, spend tens first
solutions.idea: Simulate the till with two counters. For 15 of change, use a 10 + 5 when possible, three 5s otherwise.

followups: The price is now p and customers can pay with any of k note sizes. Does spending the largest note first still always work?
Instead of true or false, return how many customers in a row you can serve if you may reorder the queue.
